plan.english: Sons of Sky, come to me!

notes: The twins' title 'sons of Sky': Ved. Divó nápātā (RV 1.117.12, 1.182.1, 1.184.1, 4.44.2, 10.61.4), Gk Διόσκουροι / Δίος παῖδες, Lith. Diẽvo sūnẽliai, Latv. Dieva dēli. The genitive of *dyḗws is shared by all three branches; the word for 'son' is renewed in each (nápāt- 'descendant', κοῦροι/παῖδες, sūnẽliai, dēli), so suHnús (the Lithuanian and common Vedic sūnú-) is interpolated. 'Come' is the Vedic root aorist ā́ gatam (gʷémt, interpolated; Alcaeus has δεῦτε). Dual throughout, as in Vedic. The Alcaeus wording follows West's citation (he prints a translation); it is not in a local corpus.

plan.english: The daughter of the Sun chose you two as husbands.

notes: The Sun's daughter and her twin suitors: Vedic sū́ro duhitā́ / sū́ryasya duhitā́ chose the Aśvins' chariot or the Aśvins as husbands (RV 1.117.13, 1.119.5, 4.43.2, 7.69.4); in the Baltic songs Lith. Sáulės dukrýtė, Latv. Saules meita is wooed by the Sons of God (LD 33766, 34008; West 2007 ch. 5). 'Daughter' and 'sun' are cognate in Vedic and Lithuanian (Latv. meita is not). The verb (*welh₁-, Ved. vṛ- middle aorist), the pronoun and pótis 'husband' (Ved. pátī) are Vedic only, interpolated.

plan.english: The two sons of Sky came, asking for the daughter of the Sun.

notes: The Sons of Sky as suitors of the Sun's daughter: RV 10.85.14 the Aśvins came 'asking for' (pṛcchámānau) Sūryā's wedding; in Latvian songs Dieva dēli are 'suitors of Saule's daughter' (LD 34008, 33766, West 2007 ch. 5). Latvian is left out of the refs to avoid a second Baltic count; its word for 'suitor' (precinieks, from precēt 'woo' < *preḱ-) would make the verb a cognate too, but the Latvian wording is not printed by West, so pr̥sḱéti (Ved. pṛccha-) is marked interpolated. Middle participle as in Vedic; 'came' is the root aorist of *gʷem- (Ved. áyātam is from yā-), interpolated. suHnús as in divine-twins-001.

plan.english: Come to us with swift horses!

notes: The inherited 'swift horses' (*h₁ōḱéwes h₁éḱwōs, Watkins 1995: 12) applied to the twin horsemen: RV 8.5.7 'come, Aśvins, with swift horses' and Alcaeus' Dioskouroi who travel over earth and sea 'on swift-footed horses' (ὠκύ-πους). Greek has the adjective inside a compound. The verb yā- 'travel, go' of the Vedic (yéh₂ti, Ved. yāti, Lith. jóti 'ride') and 'to us' are interpolated; Alcaeus has ἔρχεσθε. The Alcaeus wording follows West's citation (he prints a translation); it is not in a local corpus.

plan.english: The sons of Sky have good horses.

notes: The twins' epithet 'having good horses': Ved. su-áśva- of the Aśvins (RV 7.68.1, 69.3) and Pindar's εὔιπποι of the Tyndaridai (West 2007 ch. 4), a compound *h₁su-h₁éḱwo- in both. The compound is rendered as a phrase (dative of possession + copula). 'Horse' is shared; the prefix (Ved. su-, Gk εὐ-, from *h₁(e)su-) is a reflex of the same root as h₁wésus 'good', but not the same formation, so h₁wésus is marked interpolated, as is the possessive construction. 'Sons of Sky' as in divine-twins-001 (Pindar's Tyndaridai do not carry Zeus' name, so dyḗws is Vedic only here). Pindar's εὔιπποι is cited from West, not checked in a local corpus.

plan.english: The two sons of Sky are young.

notes: The twins are youths: Ved. yúvānā (RV 1.117.14, 3.58.7, 6.62.4, 7.67.10) beside Divó nápātā in the same hymn; the Dioskouroi are Διὸς κοῦροι 'Zeus' boys' and appear to the Romans as iuuenes (West 2007 ch. 4). Ved. yúvan- and Lat. iuuenis are the same n-stem (h₂yéwHō); the Greek word for 'boy' is different. Dual as in Vedic; 'son' as in divine-twins-001.

plan.english: Sons of Sky, you two carried him in ships.

notes: Rescuers at sea: the Aśvins carried Bhujyu out of the sea 'with ships' (naubhíḥ, RV 1.116.3, cf. the hundred-oared ship nā́vam of 1.116.5), and the Dioskouroi leap onto the masts of ships and bring light to the dark ship (Alcaeus fr. 34; Hymn. Hom. 33; West 2007 ch. 4). *néh₂us is shared; the Vedic verb vah- (*weǵʰ-, Ved. ūhathuḥ perfect, here the past of the present) and 'him' are interpolated. The Greek has no verb of carrying. The Alcaeus wording (νάων, νᾶϊ) follows West's citation (he prints a translation); it is not in a local corpus.

plan.english: The two young men came with white horses.

notes: The twin youths and their horses: RV 1.117.14 'you two young ones ... carried (Bhujyu) with swift horses', and the Roman epiphany of Castor and Pollux as two iuuenes with white horses (Cic. Nat. deor. 2.6; West 2007 ch. 4 n. 77: their horses are always white). Ved. yúvan- = Lat. iuuenis and Ved. áśva- = Lat. equus. 'White' follows the Latin (albʰós; the Vedic white horse of RV 1.116.6 is śvetá-), and 'came' (gʷémt) is interpolated; the Latin wording is cited after West's reference, not checked in a local corpus.
